summary.text: The strongest convergent signal in ulcerative colitis mucosa is the neutrophil-recruitment axis of CXCR2, CXCR1 and their ligand CXCL8. CXCR2 ranks first in the deterministic convergence ranking: it is raised in all five biopsy cohorts, local to inflamed mucosa, genetically supported in Open Targets and has clinical-stage antagonists, none established in UC. Single-cell data, however, place almost all CXCR2, CXCR1 and CXCL8 transcripts in neutrophils, and composition adjustment shrinks or removes their bulk change. The axis is therefore best read as a marker of neutrophil influx that could also be a target on recruited neutrophils, not as a change of resident tissue.

The candidates that hold up best as tissue-level targets are those whose change survives composition adjustment in a replicated cell of origin: MMP1 and CHI3L1 in inflammatory fibroblasts, IDO1 in resident macrophages and dendritic cells, and DUOX2 in enterocytes. OSMR, the oncostatin M receptor, is the only one of these with both genetic support and a clinical antibody (vixarelimab), but most of its bulk rise tracks composition, leaving a small residual stromal change.

The most reproducible biomarkers are the loss of epithelial metabolic and barrier genes (HMGCS2, SLC26A2, CLDN8), which is decreased in all five cohorts and is the only tissue-intrinsic verdict for SLC26A2, and the gain of neutrophil and antimicrobial genes (S100A8, AQP9, CHI3L1, DUOX2). These are markers of inflamed epithelium and of neutrophil infiltration rather than drug targets.

At the pathway level, JAK-STAT, TNFa and NFkB activity, and STAT3 and RELA transcription-factor activity, are raised in all five cohorts. These axes are already targeted by approved UC drugs and act as positive controls. In the trial cohorts, baseline TNFa pathway activity and genes such as OSM, IL11, TREM1 and CXCR2 are higher in ustekinumab non-responders but are also higher in placebo non-responders or show no drug-by-placebo interaction, so they mark disease severity rather than drug-specific resistance; baseline IL23A and ITGB7 do not stratify response to the drugs that target them.

expression.text: Across the five-cohort random-effects meta-analysis, the largest and most reproducible increases in UC mucosa are neutrophil-recruitment, antimicrobial and remodelling genes. The neutrophil chemokine CXCL8 rises by a pooled log2FC of [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.704], the secreted chitinase-like protein CHI3L1 by [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.714], the calprotectin subunit S100A8 by [gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.647] and the epithelial oxidase DUOX2 by [gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.3213], each significant in the same direction in all five cohorts. MMP1, MMP3, MMP7 and MMP10 follow the same pattern, a tissue-remodelling signature.

The strongest decreases describe a loss of epithelial metabolism and barrier. The tight-junction gene CLDN8 is the most strongly lost gene, with a pooled log2FC of [gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.518]; the ketogenic enzyme HMGCS2 falls by [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.5845] and the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 by [gene=SLC26A2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.496], all decreased in five of five cohorts. Together with the gain of antimicrobial and neutrophil genes, this describes a mucosa that loses colonocyte metabolism and barrier function while recruiting neutrophils; these are biomarkers of epithelial injury, not drug targets.

CXCR2, the top-ranked convergence gene, has a smaller pooled change than the chemokines, log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.264], but it is highly significant (padj [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; padj=2.94e-23]) and raised in all five cohorts. Between-cohort heterogeneity is high for most top genes, so pooled fold changes describe direction and rough size only.

inflammation.text: Within the same patients (MSCCR, paired inflamed vs non-inflamed biopsies), the neutrophil and epithelial-defence genes are clearly local to inflamed mucosa: CXCR2 rises by a paired log2FC of [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972], CHI3L1 by [gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.6182] and DUOX2 by [gene=DUOX2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.4812]. The loss of HMGCS2 is also local: it is not changed in non-inflamed mucosa versus controls (padj [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; padj=0.675]), so the epithelial metabolic loss accompanies active inflammation rather than preceding it.

A smaller component is already present in non-inflamed UC mucosa. CXCR2 is modestly but significantly raised in non-inflamed mucosa versus controls, log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.6399], and so is CHI3L1, log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.8377]. These genes therefore mark both the disease state and, much more strongly, local inflammation. The paired and non-inflamed contrasts exist only in MSCCR, so this pattern is not replicated in the microarray cohorts.

replication.text: The discovery cohort's leading changes reproduce well in the four microarray cohorts (UNIFI, PURSUIT-SC and the two Leuven cohorts): all of the leading convergence genes except CCL2 change in the same direction and significantly in all five cohorts, and CCL2 lacks a record in one cohort. For example, CXCL8 rises by [gene=CXCL8; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_control; log2fc=2.2841] in the MSCCR discovery cohort and by [gene=CXCL8; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE92415; layer=rna; cohort=GSE92415; contrast=uc_vs_control; log2fc=3.9974] in PURSUIT-SC, and HMGCS2 falls by [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-2.1465] in MSCCR and by [gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE73661; layer=rna; cohort=GSE73661; contrast=uc_vs_control; log2fc=-4.7239] in the Leuven infliximab/vedolizumab cohort. Effect sizes differ between platforms and contrasts (microarray versus RNA-seq, UC versus inflamed biopsies), so replication is judged on direction and significance rather than magnitude.

literature.text: Verbatim-validated literature relations give mechanistic support to a few expression-led candidates, each from one or two recent studies. IDO1 is elevated in UC, drives M1 macrophage polarization through the GRP78-XBP1 endoplasmic-reticulum stress pathway, and a methyl-tryptophan IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis. CHI3L1 correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression and promotes macrophage pyroptosis through BCAT1 and NF-kappaB, with velpatasvir identified as a binding repurposing hit. AQP9, predominantly neutrophil-expressed, promotes neutrophil extracellular trap formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis in mouse colitis. All three lack clinical UC data.

The literature stream is uneven. The top-ranked genes CXCR2, CXCR1 and CD274 have no extracted literature relations in the corpus, so their literature component comes only from Open Targets. Much of the biomarker literature for MMP1, DUOX2, CXCL1 and HMGCS2 is bioinformatic hub-gene or ROC analysis with little experimental validation. The most clinically relevant sentence links the inflammatory signature to treatment failure: in a single-cell tofacitinib study, non-responders upregulated IL1B together with MMP9, IL6, CXCL1, CXCL8 and S100A9.

external.text: Among genes with approved or late-stage UC drugs, JAK2 is the clearest positive control: it has a strong Open Targets association, [gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318], but only a modest biopsy change, pooled log2FC [gene=JAK2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=0.872], so it ranks below the expression-led genes. IL23A, the target of approved anti-IL-23 antibodies, ranks near the top of Open Targets UC associations but is not among the leading convergence, target or biomarker rankings, and the same holds for TNF. The biopsy-based convergence score thus favours expression-led genes over genetically and clinically validated targets. Among the leading convergence genes, CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5345]) and OSMR ([gene=OSMR; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.3907]) combine genetic support with clinical-stage drugs: CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists such as reparixin, and the anti-OSMR antibody vixarelimab.

Expression-led candidates have no genetic association in Open Targets. CXCL8 (anti-IL-8 antibodies ABX-IL8 and adakitug, phase 2) and IDO1 (epacadostat, linrodostat, developed for oncology) have drugs. CHI3L1, AQP9 and SLC26A2 have neither a genetic signal nor a clinical drug, only predicted tractability, so they are framed as biomarkers. CD274 has genetic support, but its drugs are anti-PD-L1 oncology agents whose blockade would be undesirable in an inflammatory disease. STRING places CXCR2 with CXCR1 and the ELR+ chemokines CXCL8, CXCL1 and CXCL5 in one neutrophil-recruitment module.

cells.text: Single-cell data with neutrophils (Gubatan) show that the neutrophil-axis genes leading the ranking are almost entirely neutrophil transcripts in inflamed mucosa: CXCR2 [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965], CXCR1 [gene=CXCR1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.962], AQP9 [gene=AQP9; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.92], S100A8 [gene=S100A8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.909] and CXCL8 [gene=CXCL8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.873]. The CXCR2 attribution does not replicate, because Smillie captured no neutrophils and assigns its weak signal to T/NK cells. After adjusting bulk biopsies for cell composition, CXCR2 keeps only a small residual change, adjusted log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409], and CXCL8 is no longer significant, adjusted padj [gene=CXCL8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0527]. These genes are therefore markers of neutrophil influx; a CXCR2 antagonist would act on recruited neutrophils, not on resident tissue.

Other leading candidates come from resident cells, with the lineage replicated in a second dataset, and keep a significant change after composition adjustment. MMP1 is made by inflammatory fibroblasts (dominant-lineage share [gene=MMP1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.871]; adjusted log2FC [gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636]), as is CHI3L1 ([gene=CHI3L1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.941]; adjusted [gene=CHI3L1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3967]). DUOX2 is epithelial ([gene=DUOX2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.947]; adjusted [gene=DUOX2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3161]). IDO1 comes from resident macrophages and DC1 with little neutrophil contribution ([gene=IDO1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.072]; adjusted [gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]). These are tissue changes in a defined cell type and are better target candidates than the neutrophil genes.

Two candidates sit in between. OSMR is stromal (inflammatory and WNT2B+ fibroblasts, replicated), but its change falls from an unadjusted [gene=OSMR; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; unadjusted_log2fc=1.1368] to an adjusted [gene=OSMR; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.2528], so most of its rise tracks composition with a small fibroblast-intrinsic residual. CD274 is largely neutrophil-derived in Gubatan ([gene=CD274; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.687]) but diffuse in Smillie, and retains [gene=CD274; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4978] after adjustment. The epithelial loss of SLC26A2 is the only change tested with a fully intrinsic verdict ([gene=SLC26A2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=-1.4638]). The adjustment can over-correct, because lineage scores also rise when resident cells are activated, so partly_composition and composition verdicts are not proof of pure influx.

pathways.text: Inferred pathway activity in bulk biopsies is raised in all five cohorts for JAK-STAT (largest in MSCCR, t [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE193677.t=15.68]) and TNFa (PURSUIT-SC t [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE92415.t=16.28]), with NFkB running in parallel. The downstream transcription factors STAT3 (UNIFI t [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=24.0]) and RELA (UNIFI t [type=tf_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=21.24]) are likewise active in five of five cohorts. JAK-STAT and TNF are already targeted by approved UC drugs and serve as positive controls. TGFb (UNIFI t [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE206285.t=25.17]), EGFR, hypoxia, MAPK, PI3K and VEGF are also up everywhere, so broad pathway activation in inflamed mucosa does not single out a new target.

The most specific cell-cell circuits that rise in inflamed mucosa centre on neutrophils and CXCL8, an axis that has clinical-stage CXCR2 antagonists but no UC drug. Neutrophils sending CXCL8 to ACKR1+ endothelial cells increase (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=1.991]), a plausible recruitment route through an atypical chemokine-presenting receptor, and CXCL8 from Neutrophil CXCR4 cells to neutrophils through CXCR2 increases (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.755]), an autocrine or paracrine neutrophil loop. Macrophage IL1B pairs with neutrophil IL1R2 (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.059]), but IL1R2 is a decoy receptor, so this may reflect IL-1 buffering rather than signalling. These scores are ligand-receptor co-expression, not proof of signalling.

Negative results constrain the picture. The neutrophil OSM to fibroblast circuit through IL6ST is weaker in inflamed than in uninflamed mucosa (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=-0.709]); only a Neutrophil PADI4 to fibroblast pair appears newly in inflamed tissue, from a very low base, so a neutrophil-OSM-fibroblast circuit is not supported as a leading axis here. p53 activity is lower in only three of five cohorts (for example Leuven infliximab t [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE16879.t=-3.59]), and WNT does not reach significance in the Leuven infliximab/vedolizumab cohort (padj [type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; per_cohort.GSE73661.padj=0.0637]), so neither is robust.

treatment.text: Baseline pathway activity separates responders from non-responders mainly as a marker of severity. TNFa activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000484]) and also in infliximab, golimumab, vedolizumab and UNIFI placebo non-responders, although not in the small PURSUIT placebo arm (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (PURSUIT).padj=0.932]). NFkB activity is higher in infliximab non-responders (BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.infliximab.padj=0.000294]) but equally in UNIFI placebo non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00608]). JAK-STAT (ustekinumab BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0124]; golimumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.204]) and TGFb (ustekinumab BH padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000493]; golimumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.348]) are associated with ustekinumab but not golimumab non-response, and TGFb is also significant in UNIFI placebo, so a severity component is likely.

At the gene level, the strongest ustekinumab non-response signal is IL11 (BH padj [gene=IL11; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=3.68e-8]), followed by CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=9.69e-6]), OSM ([gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000264]), TREM1 ([gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000474]) and CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000102]). None of these is drug-specific: IL11 (placebo padj [gene=IL11; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0133]), CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0126]) and TREM1 ([gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0234]) also differ in UNIFI placebo non-responders, OSM points the same way in placebo ([gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.116]), and the drug-by-placebo interaction is null for OSM ([gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.971]) and CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.973]). They mark a severe, neutrophil- and stroma-rich inflamed mucosa that responds poorly to any treatment. Baseline expression of the drug targets themselves does not predict response: IL23A for ustekinumab (BH padj [gene=IL23A; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.977]) and ITGB7 for vedolizumab (BH padj [gene=ITGB7; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.vedolizumab.padj=0.995]).

discovery.text: LAX1, a negative regulator of lymphocyte activation, is the strongest first-in-class screen candidate: raised in [gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; cohorts_up=5] cohorts, antibody-tractable and without a clinical drug. Its cell source is lymphoid, with plasma cells contributing the largest share of transcripts in inflamed mucosa ([gene=LAX1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; top_clusters_inflamed.0.share=0.433]), but the two single-cell datasets disagree on lineage (T/NK versus plasma cells). Only a small fraction of its bulk change survives composition adjustment ([gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.2299754066732223]), so the rise largely reflects lymphocyte infiltration. Missing: a replicated cell of origin, genetic support and any functional evidence that LAX1 modulation changes inflammation.

CHRDL2, a secreted BMP antagonist, is stromal (inflammatory fibroblasts) with the lineage replicated in a second dataset ([gene=CHRDL2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.939]) and is raised in [gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; cohorts_up=5] cohorts. It is antibody-tractable without a clinical drug. Only a minority of its change is retained after composition adjustment ([gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.27644631913646633]), and its vital-organ RNA is the highest among the profiled candidates ([gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=42.6]), which is a safety question. Missing: evidence that it is an activation-state gene of fibroblasts rather than a marker of fibroblast expansion, and safety profiling.

XKR9 is the screen candidate whose change is most clearly epithelial-intrinsic: most of its signal survives composition adjustment ([gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.7976121951555432]) and its vital-organ RNA is low ([gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=3.1]). It is antibody-tractable without a clinical drug. However, it is raised in only [gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; cohorts_up=2] cohorts and its lineage is not replicated in the second single-cell dataset, so replication is the missing piece before any functional work. ADGRG3, another tractable screen hit, is mostly a neutrophil transcript and was set aside as an influx marker.

integration.text: The streams agree on the neutrophil-recruitment axis. CXCR2, CXCR1 and CXCL8 are reproducibly raised and local to inflamed mucosa in expression, CXCR2 and CXCR1 have Open Targets genetic support, STRING places them in one chemokine module, the leading single-cell circuits are neutrophil CXCL8 to endothelium and to neutrophil CXCR2, and the same genes are higher in non-responders to ustekinumab and to placebo. They also agree on epithelial injury: HMGCS2, SLC26A2 and CLDN8 are lost in every cohort, and SLC26A2 loss is tissue-intrinsic. Approved axes (JAK-STAT, TNF, NFkB) recover as positive controls in pathway activity.

The streams disagree in three places. First, cell context undercuts the expression ranking: the top neutrophil genes lose most of their bulk change after composition adjustment, so their rank measures neutrophil influx more than a tissue process, whereas MMP1, CHI3L1, DUOX2 and IDO1 keep a resident-cell change. Second, genetics and expression diverge: JAK2 and IL23A, the targets of approved UC drugs, have strong Open Targets association but modest or absent biopsy signals, while CXCL8, IDO1 and CHI3L1 have large expression changes without genetic support. Third, the literature has the most mechanistic depth for IDO1, CHI3L1 and AQP9 but nothing extracted for CXCR2, CXCR1 or CD274, and the treatment data show that baseline signals of these candidates track severity rather than drug-specific resistance.

targets.rationale: Ranked first because it is the only leading gene supported by all six streams: reproducibly raised and local to inflamed mucosa, genetically supported, and with clinical-stage antagonists (reparixin, navarixin, SX-682), none established in UC. Its transcripts are almost entirely neutrophil and most of the bulk change tracks composition, so it is a marker of neutrophil influx and a target on recruited neutrophils rather than on resident tissue; its higher level in ustekinumab and placebo non-responders reflects severity.

Placed above its numeric rank because it combines a reproducible rise, local inflammation, Open Targets genetic support, a stromal cell of origin replicated in two datasets and a clinical anti-OSMR antibody (vixarelimab, phase 2). The main weakness is that most of its bulk change tracks composition, leaving a small fibroblast-intrinsic residual.

A resident-myeloid change (macrophages and DC1, little neutrophil contribution) that survives composition adjustment, with the best mechanistic literature among the candidates (M1 polarization through GRP78-XBP1; an IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis) and clinical inhibitors developed for oncology. No genetic support, and the biology is immunoregulatory, so the direction of any intervention needs experimental resolution.

A large, reproducible change made by inflammatory fibroblasts, with the lineage replicated and a significant change after composition adjustment, so it reflects stromal activation rather than influx. It is ranked below OSMR and IDO1 because it lacks genetic support and broad MMP inhibitors have a poor therapeutic record; it remains a strong tissue-remodelling biomarker.

One of the largest and most local increases, made by inflammatory fibroblasts with a change that survives adjustment, and with mechanistic literature (macrophage pyroptosis through BCAT1 and NF-kappaB). It has no genetic support and no clinical drug, so it is a strong biomarker and an exploratory target.

Positive control: JAK inhibitors are approved in UC, and JAK2 has one of the strongest Open Targets associations, but its biopsy change is modest, so it ranks below the expression-led genes. Its recovery, together with JAK-STAT pathway activity in all five cohorts, supports the validity of the analysis rather than suggesting a new target.

Ranked third numerically, but moved below the tissue-level candidates because its bulk change is no longer significant after composition adjustment and its transcripts are mostly neutrophil-derived in inflamed mucosa; it has no genetic support. It is a robust marker of neutrophil recruitment and of severity in non-responders; anti-IL-8 antibodies exist (phase 2).
An epithelial (enterocyte) gene with a large, local and replicated increase that survives composition adjustment: a marker of epithelial activation inside the tissue. No drug and no genetic support.
Lost in all five cohorts and unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa, so its loss marks active epithelial inflammation and loss of colonocyte ketogenic metabolism. A loss of function, not a target.
The only decrease tested with a fully intrinsic composition verdict: a true epithelial loss rather than dilution by infiltrating cells. A biomarker of epithelial injury, not a drug target.

A calprotectin subunit with one of the largest increases, almost entirely neutrophil-derived in inflamed mucosa; a marker of neutrophil infiltration with a small residual activation component after adjustment. Fits its established clinical use as a stool biomarker; no drug.

Ranked fourth numerically, but moved down because its cell of origin is mixed (largely neutrophil in Gubatan, diffuse in Smillie) and its drugs are anti-PD-L1 oncology agents that would be undesirable in UC. Best read as a marker of interferon-driven checkpoint feedback.

Exploratory: the leading first-in-class screen candidate, raised in all five cohorts, antibody-tractable and without a clinical drug, but its change is mostly lymphocyte infiltration and its lineage is not replicated. A hypothesis for experimental validation.

Exploratory: a stromal, antibody-tractable candidate with a replicated fibroblast lineage and a rise in all five cohorts, limited by a small composition-independent share and the highest vital-organ RNA among the screened candidates. A hypothesis for experimental validation.

limitations.text: All expression evidence comes from bulk biopsies; composition adjustment was run for only a subset of candidates (CXCR1 and AQP9 rest on cell-type attribution alone) and can over-correct when resident cells are activated rather than expanded.
Paired inflamed versus non-inflamed and non-inflamed versus control contrasts exist only in the MSCCR cohort, so the local-inflammation pattern is not replicated.
Between-cohort heterogeneity is high for most top genes and microarray fold changes are compressed, so pooled log2FC values describe direction and approximate size only.
The Smillie single-cell dataset captured no neutrophils, so neutrophil attribution (CXCR2, CXCR1, CXCL8, S100A8, AQP9) rests on the Gubatan dataset alone.
Ligand-receptor scores are co-expression, not proof of signalling; ACKR1 and IL1R2 are atypical or decoy receptors.

Treatment-response groups are small for infliximab, golimumab and vedolizumab, placebo arms are underpowered, and no gene shows a significant drug-by-placebo interaction; baseline associations are not predictions.

The literature corpus is limited and largely bioinformatic; several top genes (CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274) have no extracted relations. The PubMed connector was not authorized, so no new literature was retrieved.

Open Targets drugs are listed for any indication, and none of the listed drugs is shown to be effective in UC in these records. IL23A and TNF biopsy changes were not retrieved, so their absence from the leading rankings is not explained here.

Discovery candidates (LAX1, CHRDL2, XKR9) have no functional or genetic validation and are hypotheses only. ADGRG3, a tractable screen hit, was set aside because neutrophils make most of its transcripts.
